boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's Magdeburg entry (capitulation, 8 November 1806) in cohort v1's fourth-coalition 1806 group: the Prussian garrison of the fortress under General Kleist and Marshal Ney's 6th corps before it, from Ney's first summons and his bridge over the Elbe at Schönebeck on 23 October, through the investment, completed by 27 to 28 October, and the trial bombardment of the night of 4 to 5 November, to the armistice of 7 November, the capitulation of 8 November and the garrison's defile on 11 November. The fortress's preparation from April 1806, the disorder in the town after Jena and the search for the Hesse treasure after the capitulation are context. The remnants Prince Hohenlohe left in the garrison are counted here; his corps's capitulation is Prenzlau (B374c). Hameln (B376d) and Nienburg (B377a) are outside this entry. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side A (French) as 16,000 men under Marshal Ney, and side B (Prussian) as the garrison of 24,000 men, of whom 20,200 infantry, 500 cavalry, 2,100 artillery and 1,200 train, with 577 guns, under General of Infantry v. Kleist, which the French forced to capitulate after a 12-day investment and a short bombardment. By his stated rule his figures are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. Höpfner gives the garrison's return (claim side-b-strength), the French documents other figures (claim side-b-strength-french), and no other passage read gives side A's total (claim side-a-strength). Bodart's parts make his 24,000 (our arithmetic). They are close to Höpfner's return of 20,339 infantry, 510 cavalry, 2110 artillerymen and 1159 train, 24,118 in all, but are not that return rounded up: his total and three of his four parts are lower, and only his train is higher (our comparison). English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the heading and entry: '1806 8/11. capitulation of Magdeburg'; 'the French (16,000 men) under Marshal Ney, after a 12-day investment and a short bombardment, force the Prussian garrison (24,000 men, of whom 20,200 infantry, 500 cavalry, 2,100 artillery, 1,200 train, with 577 guns) under General of Infantry v. Kleist to capitulate, after which the whole garrison went into captivity'.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian), side A's (French) figures: Ney reported on 23 October that the adjutant-commandant who bore his summons asserted there were at least 8,000 men in the place, little siege artillery but 40 to 50 field pieces, a regiment of cuirassiers and a strong detachment of hussars. On 2 November he wrote that the garrison's strength was put that day at 15,000 men, though no very precise information had been obtained despite the questioning of the deserters who arrived daily; on 3 November, that the place held many more men than was believed, and that Baron de Williben claimed it held more than 16,000 men of all arms, a number Ney thought exaggerated. On 7 November he wrote that the men in hospital and with fever were said to number 1,800; on 8 November, that the garrison appeared to be 20,000 strong including 1,800 sick and the wounded, with about 800 guns said to be in the place, and, in a second letter, that the 20,000 including the sick and wounded had been confirmed to him. The 29th Bulletin, of 9 November, put in the fortress much artillery and 16,000 men belonging to more than 70 battalions; the Emperor wrote the same day of 16,000 men and 800 guns in the place, and the 30th Bulletin, of 10 November, of 16,000 men and nearly 800 guns fallen into French hands. After the defile on 11 November Ney wrote that each of the 4 columns exceeded 4,000 men and that, including 2,000 artillerymen, 400 cuirassiers, 20 generals and about 800 officers, the whole could be put without exaggeration at 22,000 men; the 31st Bulletin, of 12 November, gives 22,000 prisoners, among them 2,000 artillerymen.
claims.rationale: Side A's letters and Bulletins, read from the page images; the figures were checked on full-resolution crops. Not reconciled with Höpfner's return or Bodart's figures (claims side-b-strength, bodart-strength). The garrison was in the fortress before the investment, so the claim is tagged inherited. The figures run from at least 8,000 on 23 October to 22,000 at the defile, with the Emperor's letter and the 29th and 30th Bulletins at 16,000 after Ney's 20,000 of 8 November; the passages read do not show whether the differences reflect better information or a different scope, though the 20,000 includes the sick and wounded and the 22,000 the artillerymen, generals and officers. Ney's Williben of Strassfurt, a former lieutenant colonel, may be the man Höpfner calls the former Rittmeister Willisen, burgomaster of Staßfurth, whom by Höpfner's footnote Ney's report calls a former Oberstlieutenant; the passages read do not establish it. The 22,000 is also a count of the prisoners (claim side-b-losses). English renderings (ours): 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Klein Ottersleben, 23 October 1806'; 'the adjutant-commandant who bore my summons asserts that there are at least 8,000 men in the place, little siege artillery but 40 to 50 field pieces, a regiment of cuirassiers and a strong detachment of hussars'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 2 November 1806'; 'the strength of the garrison of Magdeburg is put today at 15,000 men; it has been impossible until now to obtain very precise information on this, despite the questioning to which the deserters, who arrive every day in fairly large numbers, have been subjected'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 3 November 1806'; 'this work, on which the engineer officers have been busy for 4 days, will prove to Your Highness that the whole of the troops is not too numerous to blockade a place that holds many more men than is believed and that must be watched very closely, to deprive it of the resources in subsistence it could draw from its surroundings'; 'Baron de Williben, former lieutenant colonel in the service of Prussia, president of the first circle of the administration of Magdeburg, who lives at Strassfurt, has been appointed commissioner by the civil authorities of the province to go to Berlin to Your Highness and, if possible, to His Majesty, to obtain that the place not be bombarded'; 'this officer has made vain efforts to convince Count Kleist that the obstinacy of the defence is pointless in the present circumstances; he claims that the place holds more than 16,000 men of all arms; I think this number exaggerated'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. claims.value: Side A (French): Bodart gives 16,000 men under Marshal Ney. Höpfner: Ney's corps hardly had the strength of the garrison, and at the moment only 900 cavalry at its disposal. Ney's order for the passage of the Elbe of 23 October names the 3rd division, the army's park and the headquarters baggage, General Klein's 2 dragoon regiments, the 76th and 69th regiments with the 2nd division's artillery and baggage, the 39th, the 10th chasseurs and the 6th light. On 25 October Ney wrote that Vandamme had taken command of the 3rd division; that Klein had only 2 dragoon regiments, the 1st and the 14th, together 700 mounted men, having detached 3 regiments to Nordhausen by the Grand Duke's order; that the 10th chasseurs had at most 200 horses and the 3rd hussars had stayed at Erfurt; and that escorts for prisoners and deserters greatly reduced his cavalry; he asked for one more regiment of light cavalry out of the most pressing need. On 3 November he wrote that by the major general's orders he had redirected the 2 dragoon regiments to Berlin, Klein going to rejoin General Picard's brigade and go to Berlin with his division; that Vandamme's division was absolutely insufficient to blockade Magdeburg on both banks; that on the right bank there was not a quarter of the troops needed; and that the whole of his troops was not too numerous for the blockade. For the raid of the night of 31 October to 1 November Ney's daily report gives General Colbert 600 men of the 6th light and 2 voltigeur companies of the 39th, supported by 1 squadron of hussars and chasseurs and 2 four-pounders, and Höpfner gives General Kolbert 600 light infantry, 2 voltigeur companies and 2 squadrons; both place 6 grenadier companies at Schönebeck. On 8 November Ney wrote that a detachment of the 3rd hussars, some voltigeur companies and a grenadier battalion of his corps were being sent from Erfurt, to arrive on the 13th, and that the rest of the voltigeurs and hussars used to escort the prisoners would leave Erfurt on the 8th. No passage read gives a count of side A's infantry or a total for Ney's corps.
claims.rationale: Bodart from the frame transcription; Höpfner, Ney's letters and his daily report read from the page images, the figures checked on full-resolution crops. The corps was brought to Magdeburg before the investment, and its cavalry was reduced by orders from above (the Grand Duke's detachment to Nordhausen, the major general's order sending the dragoons to Berlin), so the claim is tagged inherited. Höpfner's 900 cavalry equal Ney's 700 dragoons and 200 chasseurs of 25 October (our arithmetic); whether he took them from Ney's letter is not shown, and by 3 November the dragoons had been sent away. Whether the light cavalry regiment Ney asked for was sent is not shown. The daily report is Ney's: his signature closes it on p. 645. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; 'Ney's corps hardly had the strength of the garrison, and at the moment only 900 men of cavalry at its disposal, but the governor had too little confidence in his men to bring himself to an active defence'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Klein Ottersleben, 23 October 1806'; 'I have the honour to report to Your Highness that I am having a bridge of boats built at Schönebeck; as soon as this operation is finished, I shall cross the Elbe to seize on the right bank of that river all the communications that lead to Magdeburg'; 'the passage will take place in the following manner'; 'the 3rd division will open the march; then the army's park and the headquarters baggage; General Klein's 2 dragoon regiments; the 76th and 69th regiments, the artillery and the baggage of the 2nd division; the 39th and the 10th chasseurs. The march will be closed by the 6th light'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 25 October 1806'; 'General Vandamme has arrived at the army corps and taken command of the 3rd division'; 'General Klein is also with me; but he has only 2 dragoon regiments, the 1st and the 14th, making together 700 mounted men. This general has detached 3 regiments to Nordhausen to scour the country and gather up escaped prisoners. This disposition was ordered by the Grand Duke'; 'the 10th chasseurs has at most 200 horses, and the 3rd hussars stayed at Erfurt to escort the prisoners'; 'convoys of prisoners and deserters, which reach me every day, require escorts that greatly reduce my cavalry'; 'I beg Your Highness to have one more regiment of light cavalry sent to me, if possible. This request is prompted by the most pressing need'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 3 November 1806'; 'in accordance with your orders, I have changed the direction of the 2 dragoon regiments that spent last night at Nedlitz, on the Brandenburg road, to go to Berlin'; 'General Picard's brigade must have crossed the Elbe today at Dessau; I have'; 'informed General Klein of it, who answered me that he would rejoin that brigade and go to Berlin with his division united'; 'General Vandamme's division is absolutely insufficient to blockade Magdeburg on both banks of the Elbe, the extent of the fortifications being immense. I have gone over all the positions that it is indispensable to occupy: those of the right bank require fewer men, yet there is not a quarter of the troops needed at that point; and in case of a sortie General Colbert would be forced to fall back on Pechau and Gommern while awaiting the help I would send him from the 2nd division'; 'this work, on which the engineer officers have been busy for 4 days, will prove to Your Highness that the whole of the troops is not too numerous to blockade a place that holds many more men than is believed and that must be watched very closely, to deprive it of the resources in subsistence it could draw from its surroundings'; 'daily report on the blockade of Magdeburg. claims.value: Bodart names Marshal Ney as side A's (French) commander and General of Infantry v. Kleist as side B's (Prussian). The capitulation Foucart prints was agreed between General of Brigade Dutaillis, with Colonel Ligor-Belair and Captain Regnard named in parentheses, stipulating in the name of Marshal Ney, and Major General de Renouard, with du Troussel and Leblanc named in parentheses, stipulating in the name of Count de Kleist, general of infantry and military governor of the town and citadel of Magdeburg.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed commanders and the capitulation's preamble, read from the page images. Höpfner calls Kleist the governor and Colonel dü Trossel the commandant (claim side-b-command); Ney's letter of 23 October and the armistice's preamble call Kleist lieutenant general, and General Marchand's letter of 2 November lieutenant general (claim side-a-information), while the capitulation and Höpfner call him general of infantry. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; the capitulation, 'articles of capitulation for the town and fortress of Magdeburg, agreed between General of Brigade Dutaillis, one of the commanders of the Legion of Honour, knight of the military order of Bavaria, and chief of the general staff of the 6th corps of the French Grande Armée in Germany (the'; 'Colonel Ligor-Belair and Captain Regnard), etc., stipulating in the name of Marshal of the Empire Ney'; 'and Messrs. de Renouard, major general, chief of an infantry regiment and knight of the order of Military Merit of Prussia (du Troussel and Leblanc), stipulating in the name of His Excellency Count de Kleist, general of infantry, knight of the orders of the Black Eagle and of the Red Eagle of Prussia and of that of Saint Alexander Nevsky of Russia, and military governor of the town and citadel of Magdeburg'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. claims.value: Höpfner and Ney's letters: on 23 October Ney had a bridge of boats built at Schönebeck, to cross the Elbe and seize all the communications reaching Magdeburg on the right bank, and summoned the governor, who refused. When Soult left for Tangermünde, Ney relieved the 4th corps's posts before Magdeburg on the left bank and wrote on 25 October that General Colbert's light troops would cross the Elbe at Schönebeck the next day to form the investment on the right bank; Höpfner has him move his headquarters to Schönebeck and complete the investment on the right bank on the 27th, though still at a great distance from the place. By Ney's daily report of 2 November his troops drove the enemy's advanced posts under the cannon of the place from the 26th to the 28th, completing the blockade; Vandamme had some thirty shells fired into the town in the night of the 29th, which did not set it on fire (Höpfner: some shells, which did not set it alight); small posts were carried on the 30th and 31st; in the night of 31 October to 1 November Colbert surrounded the villages of Crakau and Prester at 3 in the morning and set fire to the farms holding produce, Marchand had a post of 15 grenadiers carried, and a general reconnaissance went up to the ditches of the place; and, Ney wrote, the alarms he gave from time to time would tire the garrison still more. Höpfner has Kolbert drive the Prussian outposts into the fortress and the French posts pushed to 12—1500 paces from the glacis. Ney had the orders of the day announcing the capture of Prince Hohenlohe's corps and the surrender of Stettin spread in the town, and, by Höpfner, sent the governor the French Bulletin containing the capitulation of Prenzlau. He asked for mortars on 30 October, and the 4 he had asked of General Clarke arrived on 2 November. On 7 November he reported his troops and outposts entrenched, communications cut, his artillery placed to sweep the plain, and fire almost every night and signal rockets twice each night, alarms that exhausted the garrison. In the night of 4 to 5 November 12 bombs and some shells were fired on the place (Höpfner and Ney), burning one house in the town and 2 in the Neustadt suburb (Ney). Ney made his last summons on the 5th, saying, by Höpfner, that the bombardment had only been meant to prove that he had the means to reduce Magdeburg to ashes. On 6 November he sent his aide-de-camp Liger-Belair and Captain Regnard into Magdeburg with Major Wedell (Höpfner); by Ney's letters the parleys began on the 6th, he sent a draft capitulation on the 7th, Liger-Belair and Regnard signed the armistice of 7 November for side A, and he cut short the delay the governor asked for, so that the garrison would defile on the 11th. The capitulation was agreed in Ney's name by General of Brigade Dutaillis, chief of the general staff of the 6th corps, with Colonel Ligor-Belair and Captain Regnard (Höpfner's Dütaillis came into the fortress on the afternoon of the 8th), and signed, Ney wrote, on the evening of the 8th.
claims.rationale: Höpfner, Ney's letters, his daily report and the armistice and capitulation texts, read from the page images. These were the steps of side A's commander and his generals at Magdeburg, so the claim is tagged commander-created; the bridge over the Elbe was also the major general's order, which Ney says on 3 November had been renewed (claim posture). Höpfner gives Ney's efforts to obtain mortars from Ney's correspondence captured at Gutstadt in 1807 (his footnote). Höpfner has Kolbert drive the outposts into the fortress; Ney's report says the enemy had withdrawn its small posts the night before. English renderings (ours): 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Klein Ottersleben, 23 October 1806'; 'I have the honour to report to Your Highness that I am having a bridge of boats built at Schönebeck; as soon as this operation is finished, I shall cross the Elbe to seize on the right bank of that river all the communications that lead to Magdeburg'; 'I have had Lieutenant General de Kleist, governor of Magdeburg, summoned; his answer was negative'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 25 October 1806'; 'Marshal Soult set out this morning with his army corps in the direction of Tangermünde; the aim of this movement is to close the passage of the Elbe to the Duke of Weimar'; 'I have accordingly had all the posts that the 4th corps held before Magdeburg on the left bank of the Elbe relieved'; 'a corps of light troops under General Colbert will cross the Elbe tomorrow at Schönebeck to form the investment of Magdeburg on the right bank of that river'; 'on 23 October Marshal Ney, whose headquarters had until then been at Groß-Ottersleben, had a bridge of boats thrown over the Elbe at Schönebeck, which was passable on the 25th'; 'Marshal Soult's departure for Tangermünde allowed only an observation of the fortress, for which Marshal Ney moved his headquarters to Schönebeck'; 'only on the 27th did he complete the investment on the right bank of the Elbe, though still at a great distance from the place'; 'daily report on the blockade of Magdeburg. Schönebeck, 2 November 1806'; 'the 26th, 27th and 28th were spent compelling the enemy's advanced posts on both banks of the Elbe to withdraw immediately under the cannon of the place; from then on the blockade was complete'; 'in the night of the 29th General Vandamme had some thirty shells fired, which fell in the town without setting it on fire. The enemy replied with his heavy artillery, but without any effect'; 'on the 29th they began to have some buildings pulled down that hindered the defence of the Sudenburg and the Neustadt; the rest was burned down in the night. The enemy'; 'did not interfere; in general it had so far come only to insignificant engagements'; 'in the same night General Vandamme had some shells thrown at the town, which, however, did not set it alight'; 'the 30th and the 31st were spent carrying some small enemy posts; some thirty men were taken, and as many killed or wounded. We had 2 men killed and 3 wounded'; 'in the night of the 31st to 1 November General Colbert, with 600 men of the 6th light and 2 voltigeur companies of the 39th, supported by 1 squadron of hussars and chasseurs and 2 four-pounders, approached Friedrichstadt out of cannon range and surrounded the villages of Crakau and Prester, as well as all the farms nearer the place'; 'this operation took place at 3 in the morning; the enemy had withdrawn all his small forward posts during the night before. Fire was set to all the farms that'; 'held produce, so that the enemy can no longer draw any help from them'; 'in the same night of the 31st to 1 November General Marchand had an enemy post of 15 grenadiers, furnished by that of the Closterberg, carried; the enemy also had 4 killed and 6 wounded. We had neither killed nor wounded'; 'a general reconnaissance combined with General Vandamme's troops took place that same night along the whole length of the blockade line on the left bank of the Elbe and up to the ditches of the place. Its main object was to carry posts, but the enemy had taken the precaution of withdrawing them at the evening gun. The musketry was fairly brisk; we had neither killed nor wounded'; 'it is known that the garrison is tired of its service; it will be still more so through the alarms that we give it from time to time'; 'Marshal Ney'; 'General Kolbert, who commanded on the right bank, gathered in the following night 600 men of light infantry, 2 companies of voltigeurs and 2 squadrons, attacked the Prussian outposts at 3 o'clock in the morning of 1 November, drove them back into the fortress and set fire to the villages of Krakau and Prester'; 'the French posts on the right bank were now pushed forward to a distance of 12—1500 paces from the glacis, the supports in Biederitz, Alt- and Neu-Königsborn, Menz, Gübs and Pechau, reserves at Gerwisch, Woltersdorf, Nedlitz and Gommern'; 'Marshal Ney sent the governor of Magdeburg, through the former Rittmeister Willisen, burgomaster of Staßfurth, the French Bulletin that contained the capitulation of Prenzlau, and had the impossibility of a relief represented to him'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 2 November 1806'; 'I had the honour of writing to you on 30 October and asking you for some mortars to bombard Magdeburg; it would be all the more essential for me to have them at my disposal as the persons with whom I have intelligences in the place are only waiting for the moment when I have had bombs thrown, to force the governor, Count Kleist, to capitulate'; 'I have taken care to have the orders of the day announcing the capture of Prince Hohenlohe's army corps, the surrender of Stettin, etc., brought into the town and spread there'; 'P.S. — The 4 mortars I asked General Clarke for have just reached me this instant with their supply'; 'taken from the correspondence of Marshal Ney to Napoleon intercepted at Gutstadt in 1807, from which it also appears that the marshal made every arrangement to see some mortars brought before Magdeburg as quickly as possible'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 7 November 1806'; 'the troops are entrenched in their positions, as are the advanced posts: cuts have been made on various communications that the number of my troops did not allow me to guard: the artillery is placed on the flank and on the front of the divisions to sweep the plain and protect the withdrawal of the outposts in case of a sortie; in short, every measure has been taken to cut the enemy off from all communication with the outside and to take from him the means of foraging'; 'musketry and cannonade are repeated almost every night between Neustadt and Diesdorf, which tired the garrison of Magdeburg extremely. I have signal rockets fired twice each'; 'night. All these alarms exhaust the enemy, so that the deserters and prisoners say that the garrison has only one night of rest, during which it is often obliged to take up arms'; 'on the 5th I made my last summons to the governor, and on the 6th the parleys began. I have today sent a draft capitulation; M. de Kleist has assembled his council of war; it seems that opinions there are divided; but despite the delays this causes, I hope to have a definite answer shortly'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 7 November 1806' (his second letter of that date); 'in the night of the 4th to the 5th the 2nd division took up arms. The 3rd division was also under arms all night; the enemy attempted a sortie between 8 and 9 o'clock; he was sharply repulsed. 12 bombs and some shells were fired on the place; one house was burned in the town and 2 others in the suburb of Neustadt'; 'on 4 November the enemy attacked the Neustadt but was repulsed, and in the night to the 5th Marshal Ney had 12 bombs and also some shells thrown at the Altstadt and the Neustadt from the 4 mortars brought up meanwhile from Erfurt, and had the Neustadt attacked repeatedly in vain'; 'on the afternoon of the 5th Marshal Ney summoned the fortress again, with the remark that by the bombardment he had only wanted to prove that he possessed the means to reduce Magdeburg to ashes; at the same time he again recalled the misfortunes of the Prussian army and the impossibility of a relief, and asked the governor to have regard for the unfortunate 25,000 inhabitants, who would be exposed to the misfortune of a bombardment to no benefit for the state' (pp. 333-334); 'on 6 November the marshal sent his aide-de-camp Liger-Belair and Captain Regnard to Magdeburg, accompanied by Major Wedell of the Leib-Kürassier regiment, who had been taken prisoner at Prenzlau'; 'Marshal Ney to the Emperor. Schönebeck, 8 November 1806'; 'I have the honour to lay before Your Majesty a copy of the armistice concluded last night with the governor of Magdeburg'; 'I have at this moment officers in the place who are settling the conditions of the capitulation on the basis already agreed, that the garrison will be prisoner and sent to France, except the officers, who will return home on parole'; 'the governor asked for a delay for his arrangements; I have shortened it, and it will defile on the 11th'; 'done in duplicate at Magdeburg, 7 November 1806'; 'the adjutant-commandant, chief of staff of the advance guard of the 6th corps of the Grande Armée, Liger-Belair'; 'the captain aide-de-camp of His Excellency Marshal Ney, Regnard'; 'Marshal Ney to the Emperor. Schönbeck, 8 November 1806' (his second letter of that date); 'the fortress of Magdeburg surrenders to Your Majesty's arms; the capitulation was signed this evening; I have the honour to lay it before you'; 'articles of capitulation for the town and fortress of Magdeburg, agreed between General of Brigade Dutaillis, one of the commanders of the Legion of Honour, knight of the military order of Bavaria, and chief of the general staff of the 6th corps of the French Grande Armée in Germany (the'; 'Colonel Ligor-Belair and Captain Regnard), etc., stipulating in the name of Marshal of the Empire Ney'; 'on the 8th General Dütaillis, chief of staff of Marshal Ney, came into the fortress in the afternoon, and at 1 o'clock the capitulation was concluded'.

claims.value: Höpfner: the governor, General of Infantry von Kleist, was 73 and deprived of the use of part of his limbs by age, illness, wounds and the hardships of war; after ordering everything himself by day and night in the first days he collapsed into slackness, and he had turned his confidence chiefly to General Count Wartensleben, who seems to have wished early on for a speedy surrender and, by Ney's report, is said to have told the French parlementaire on 23 October to throw bombs and shells into the town to change the governor's mind. Ney's letter of 23 October has Wartensleben tell adjutant-commandant Lefol in confidence that he hoped to bring the governor to reason if a few shells were fired on the place. The commandant, Colonel dü Trossel, stood in complete dependence on the governor and was seldom told of negotiations or orders. Kleist had neglected to supply the fortress with fresh meat and other provisions from the right bank in the 10 days from 18 to 27 October, for which, Höpfner says, the confusion in the fortress until the Hohenlohe troops had left may at first have been to blame, and he had too little confidence in his men to bring himself to an active defence. He refused Ney's summons of 23 October, giving his word, Ney wrote, not to thwart French movements out of range of his cannon, and asked on the 27th for a meeting, held with Vandamme on the 28th without result. On the 29th the defenders began to pull down buildings that hindered the defence of the Sudenburg and Neustadt and burned the rest in the night, and on the 31st the garrison foraged along the right bank (Höpfner; Ney's report gives a sortie of about 600 infantry, 50 cuirassiers and 2 guns, which carried off 6 wagons of forage). Kleist asked Ney to let an officer go to Berlin to learn the situation of the Prussian army, proposing a cessation of arms until the officer's return, but did not accept Ney's condition that the town surrender once it was proved that no Prussian army remained (Ney, 2 and 3 November; Höpfner gives the request as his answer to the summons of the 5th). On 6 November he assembled the generals present and the commandant, laid the correspondence with Ney before them, had Major Wedell give an account of the army's march to the Oder and announced his decision to capitulate; he asked no advice, curtly rejected all objections, silencing Major General v. Alvensleben, who asked what they had been called for and said that they still lacked nothing, and formally ordered the meeting to sign the protocol. Höpfner writes that a formal council of war, to which by regulation all the garrison's staff officers had to be called, was rightly expected to follow, and that the negotiations went on; neither the engineer of the place, Captain Kleist, nor the artillery officer of the place, Major Hüser, was called to the conference. When the engineer represented that the fortress could hold 4—5 weeks after the opening of the trenches, Kleist answered that Wedell had convinced him that relief was hopeless and that he must capitulate out of humanity. All the generals except Wartensleben had shown themselves more or less averse to surrender. The armistice of 7 November was signed for side B by Colonel du Troussel and Captain Le Blanc (Foucart's text; Höpfner names General Renouard, dü Trossel and Leblank), and the capitulation was agreed in Kleist's name by Major General de Renouard with du Troussel and Leblanc. Ney wrote on 7 November that Kleist had assembled his council of war, where opinions seemed divided, and on 8 November that the governor raised difficulties up to the signing, the magistrates and inhabitants wishing to capitulate and the officers insisting on resistance. The 29th Bulletin says that when several houses had been burned in the bombardment the inhabitants showed their discontent and the commandant asked to capitulate.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images of pp. 331-335, with Ney's letters, his daily report, the armistice and capitulation texts and the 29th Bulletin from the page images. These were the governor's decisions at Magdeburg, so the claim is tagged commander-created. Höpfner takes Wartensleben's words from Ney's report to Napoleon, from the correspondence captured at Gutstadt in 1807 (his footnote), and in this section cites the records of the inquiry into the capitulation (claim side-b-information). The armistice Foucart prints is signed for side B by du Troussel and Le Blanc only; Höpfner adds Renouard, who in Foucart's text heads side B's agents for the capitulation. The Bulletin's 'commandant' is not named in the passage read; Höpfner gives that title to dü Trossel and calls Kleist the governor. Höpfner's account of the meeting of 6 November and Ney's mention of a council of war on the 7th are kept as given; the passages read do not show whether they describe one meeting. English renderings (ours): 'governor of Magdeburg was the General of Infantry von Kleist, an old man of 73, who had greatly distinguished himself in earlier wars, especially at the siege of Mainz, but was now deprived of the use of part of his limbs by age, illness, wounds and the hardships of war'; 'nevertheless he had summoned up all his strength and in the first days ordered everything personally by day and by night, but only to collapse afterwards into all the greater slackness, to which were added grief at the misfortune of the state and vexation at the dissolution of all discipline, all of which had shaken him deeply, who had grown great in the old strict Prussian school'; 'for the rest the governor was a proud, hard man, feared by his subordinates, who at this time, however, had turned his confidence chiefly to General Count Wartensleben, who had stayed behind in the fortress, who seems early on to have wished for a speedy surrender and, according to Marshal Ney's report to Napoleon, is said to have told the French parlementaire, who complained to him of the old governor's obstinacy, as early as 23 October: "First throw plenty of bombs and shells into the town, and the obstinate governor will surely change his mind."'; 'taken from the correspondence of Marshal Ney to Napoleon intercepted at Gutstadt in 1807, from which it also appears that the marshal made every arrangement to see some mortars brought before Magdeburg as quickly as possible'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Klein Ottersleben, 23 October 1806'; 'General Wartensleben, sent by the King of Prussia to this governor, told adjutant-commandant Lefol in confidence that he hoped to succeed in making him listen to reason if a few shells were fired on the place'; 'commandant was Colonel dü Trossel, who stood in complete dependence on the governor and was seldom informed by him of any negotiations and orders'; 'of bread flour there was a stock for 3 months; of grain there could be no lack, given the great stores in this trading town; on the other hand the governor had neglected, in the 10 days from 18 to 27 October, when the complete investment first took place, to supply himself from the rich country on the right bank of the Elbe with sufficient fresh meat and the other provisions, for which the confusion in the fortress until the complete departure of the Hohenlohe troops may at first have been to blame'; 'Ney's corps hardly had the strength of the garrison, and at the moment only 900 men of cavalry at its disposal, but the governor had too little confidence in his men to bring himself to an active defence'; 'I have had Lieutenant General de Kleist, governor of Magdeburg, summoned; his answer was negative'; 'M. de Kleist has moreover given his word not to seek to thwart the operations of the French armies provided the movements take place out of range of his cannon'; 'as early as the 23rd the marshal had summoned the governor to surrender; the governor asked on the 27th for a meeting, which took place on the 28th between him and General Vandamme but had no result'; 'on the 29th they began to have some buildings pulled down that hindered the defence of the Sudenburg and the Neustadt; the rest was burned down in the night. The enemy'; 'on the 31st the garrison made a foraging expedition along the right bank of the Elbe towards the Herrenkrug'; 'daily report on the blockade of Magdeburg. Schönebeck, 2 November 1806'; 'on the 31st the enemy made a sortie by Friedrichstadt, on the right bank of the Elbe; it was made up of about 600 infantry, 50 cuirassiers and 2 guns. The enemy, after forming up in line between Crakau and Prester, carried off 6 wagons of forage and went back into the place immediately afterwards'; 'Marshal Ney'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 2 November 1806'; 'the governor expressed to me the wish to send one of his officers to Berlin to learn the situation of the Prussian army, so as to take a decision either for the defence of the place or for the capitulation. I had agreed to this request on the condition that on this officer's return the town would capitulate. The governor has not spoken of it again'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 3 November 1806'; 'the governor renewed to me yesterday the request for a passport for one of his aides-de-camp, whom he wished to send'; 'to Berlin to make sure of the situation of the Prussian armies; he proposed a cessation of arms until this officer's return. I offered this passage on the condition that the town would surrender as soon as it was proved that there was no longer a Prussian army; this condition was not accepted'; Höpfner, as in claim side-a-command for the summons of the 5th; 'the governor answered: he could not enter into anything until he had really convinced himself of the dissolution of the army by sending a Prussian officer; until that officer's return, however, he would conclude an armistice'; 'on 6 November the marshal sent his aide-de-camp Liger-Belair and Captain Regnard to Magdeburg, accompanied by Major Wedell of the Leib-Kürassier regiment, who had been taken prisoner at Prenzlau'; 'the governor at once assembled the generals present in Magdeburg and the commandant, laid before them the correspondence with Marshal Ney, had Major Wedell give an account of the events in the army on the march to the Oder, and announced his decision to capitulate'; 'the way in which the governor handled the whole matter seemed to be nothing more than a communication of his decision; he asked no advice of the generals, curtly rejected all objections, and formally ordered the meeting to sign the protocol drawn up'; 'when General Alvensleben asked what they had actually been called for, and remarked that they still lacked nothing, that they all still had red cheeks etc., the governor silenced him with the words: "Major General v. claims.value: Bodart records the capitulation of Magdeburg on 8 November, after which the whole garrison went into captivity, 16 generals and 800 officers being released on parole. Höpfner: on the afternoon of the 7th an armistice was signed and all work in the fortress stopped; on the 8th General Dütaillis, Ney's chief of staff, came into the fortress in the afternoon, and at 1 o'clock the capitulation was concluded; on the 10th the French occupied the Ulrich gate, and on the 11th the garrison laid down its arms and was marched to Bernburg in 4 equally strong columns, each escorted by 6 companies of infantry and 20 cavalrymen, an infantry regiment following in reserve. The armistice Foucart prints, made between Marshal Ney and Lieutenant General Count de Kleist as being agreed on the main points of the capitulation that was to put the place and citadel in the French army's power, runs from 7 November and was done at Magdeburg that day; on 8 November Ney sent a copy of the armistice concluded 'last night' and wrote that his officers in the place were settling the capitulation on the basis already agreed, that the garrison would be prisoners and sent to France except the officers, who would return home on parole, and that it would defile on the 11th. In a second letter that day he wrote that the fortress surrendered and the capitulation had been signed that evening. Its articles 1 to 4 hand over the town, citadel and fortifications with their artillery, munitions, magazines, supplies and public property; give the Ulrich gate and its outworks to the French on 10 November in the afternoon; have the garrison march out by the Ulrich gate on the morning of 11 November with the honours of war and 4 field pieces and lay down its arms; and make it prisoners of war, the soldiers to be taken to France and the officers prisoners on parole not to serve before exchange, free to go where they chose, those with families who were settled and married in Magdeburg being allowed to stay. Its date line is Magdeburg, 8 November 1806. The 29th Bulletin, of 9 November, says the commandant asked to capitulate after the bombardment; the Emperor wrote that day that Magdeburg had surrendered on the 7th; the 30th Bulletin, of 10 November, that it surrendered on the 8th and its gates were occupied by the French on the 9th. Ney reported on 11 November that the garrison, in 4 columns, began to defile at 9 in the morning and finished at 3 in the afternoon, each column being sent to Bernburg under an escort of 6 companies of infantry under a chef de bataillon and 25 cavalrymen, with General Roguet in overall command; Roguet's memoirs, in Foucart's footnote, give him 18 companies under 3 chefs de bataillon and 2 guns, and say the operation was finished only at 6 in the evening and that he organised 8 columns. The 31st Bulletin: the garrison defiled on the 11th at 9 in the morning before Ney's corps. The Emperor congratulated Ney on 12 November on the happy surrender of Magdeburg.
claims.rationale: The frozen frame outcome with Höpfner's account and the French documents, read from the page images (Bodart's from the frame transcription); no source read gives a different result. The second figure of the hour in article 3 is damaged in print and is not read (the transcription writes it '[?]'), so the hour is not restated; articles 5 to 18 were not transcribed. The date and the timings differ and are kept as given: the capitulation is dated 8 November by Bodart, Höpfner, Ney's letters, its own date line and the 30th Bulletin, and 'the 7th', the armistice's date, by the Emperor's letter of 9 November; Höpfner's 'at 1 o'clock' after an arrival in the afternoon does not say which 1 o'clock, and Ney says the capitulation was signed in the evening; Höpfner has the armistice signed on the afternoon of the 7th, Ney's letter 'last night'; the gates were to be occupied on the 10th (article 2; Höpfner), but the 30th Bulletin has them occupied on the 9th; and the defile ran from 9 to 3 in 4 columns with 25 cavalrymen each (Ney), in 4 columns with 20 (Höpfner), or until 6 in the evening in 8 columns (Roguet). claims.value: Side A's (French) loss in Ney's reports: his daily report of 2 November says the enemy's heavy cannonade on his entrenched posts caused neither killed nor wounded from the 26th to the 28th, nor on the 29th at Vandamme's posts; that on the 30th and 31st, in carrying small posts, his troops had 2 men killed and 3 wounded; and that in the night of 31 October to 1 November Marchand's raid and the general reconnaissance cost neither killed nor wounded. On 7 November he wrote that the enemy, after several sorties, had not managed to take a single prisoner from his troops. No passage read gives a French loss for the days from 3 November to the capitulation, including the fighting at the Neustadt on 4 November and in the night to the 5th, or a total for side A, and Bodart prints none.
claims.rationale: Side A's reports, read from the page images. They cover only parts of the investment and are not a total; Colbert's raid of the same night is given no loss. For the night of 4 to 5 November Ney's letter of 7 November reports a Prussian sortie sharply repulsed, and Höpfner French attacks on the Neustadt repulsed and repeated in vain, neither with a French loss (claim posture). English renderings (ours): 'daily report on the blockade of Magdeburg. Schönebeck, 2 November 1806'; 'the 26th, 27th and 28th were spent compelling the enemy's advanced posts on both banks of the Elbe to withdraw immediately under the cannon of the place; from then on the blockade was complete'; 'the enemy cannonaded our posts heavily; but as they are entrenched, there were neither killed nor wounded'; 'on the 29th the same cannonade by the enemy on the posts of General Vandamme, entrenched within musket range of Neustadt: neither killed nor wounded'; 'the 30th and the 31st were spent carrying some small enemy posts; some thirty men were taken, and as many killed or wounded. We had 2 men killed and 3 wounded'; 'in the same night of the 31st to 1 November General Marchand had an enemy post of 15 grenadiers, furnished by that of the Closterberg, carried; the enemy also had 4 killed and 6 wounded. We had neither killed nor wounded'; 'a general reconnaissance combined with General Vandamme's troops took place that same night along the whole length of the blockade line on the left bank of the Elbe and up to the ditches of the place. Its main object was to carry posts, but the enemy had taken the precaution of withdrawing them at the evening gun. The musketry was fairly brisk; we had neither killed nor wounded'; 'Marshal Ney'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 7 November 1806'; 'great exactness reigns in the service, and the result is that the enemy, after attempting several sorties, has not managed to take a single prisoner from us'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 7 November 1806' (his second letter of that date); 'in the night of the 4th to the 5th the 2nd division took up arms. The 3rd division was also under arms all night; the enemy attempted a sortie between 8 and 9 o'clock; he was sharply repulsed. 12 bombs and some shells were fired on the place; one house was burned in the town and 2 others in the suburb of Neustadt'; 'on 4 November the enemy attacked the Neustadt but was repulsed, and in the night to the 5th Marshal Ney had 12 bombs and also some shells thrown at the Altstadt and the Neustadt from the 4 mortars brought up meanwhile from Erfurt, and had the Neustadt attacked repeatedly in vain'.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian) lost the fortress and its garrison. Bodart: the whole garrison went into captivity, 16 generals and 800 officers being released on parole, and besides the 577 guns the French took 1 million pounds of powder, 80,000 filled bombs, 54 flags and 5 standards. Höpfner, from Ney's report: 22,000 men of all arms, 20 generals and 800 officers were taken in Magdeburg, with 700 cannon, 1 million pounds of powder, 80,000 filled bombs, iron in abundance, a pontoon train, 54 flags and 5 standards and several silver trumpets, and 346 foreign flags and 10 such standards were found in the arsenal; among the guns were 39 position guns of the field artillery. He names the generals present at the governor's conference and the others taken prisoner. Ney, 11 November: each of the 4 columns exceeded 4,000 men, and with 2,000 artillerymen, 400 cuirassiers, 20 generals and about 800 officers the whole could be put without exaggeration at 22,000 men; he held 54 infantry flags and 5 standards, others having been broken; the fortress held 700 guns, a million livres of powder, a very great quantity of cast iron, a train of 90 pontoons and flour. The 30th Bulletin: 16,000 men, nearly 800 guns and magazines of every kind fell into French hands. The 31st Bulletin: 20 generals, 800 officers, 22,000 prisoners, among them 2,000 artillerymen, 54 flags, 5 standards, 800 guns, a million of powder, a great bridge train and an immense matériel of artillery. Roguet's memoirs, in Foucart's footnote, say that 20,000 prisoners reached the Rhine. Before the capitulation, Ney's daily report gives some thirty men taken and as many killed or wounded on the 30th and 31st, and a post of 15 grenadiers carried by Marchand, with 4 more killed and 6 wounded, in the night of 31 October to 1 November.
claims.rationale: Separate accounts read from the page images (Bodart's from the frame transcription), not combined. Bodart's powder, bombs, flags and standards are the figures Höpfner gives from Ney's report, but his guns are the 577 of Höpfner's garrison return, not the report's 700 (our comparison); which source Bodart used was not checked. Ney's letter of 11 November and the report Höpfner cites agree on 22,000 men, 20 generals, 800 officers, 700 guns, a million of powder, 54 flags and 5 standards, but the letter read has no bombs, trumpets or arsenal flags, so Höpfner's report may be another document or a fuller copy (not checked). Höpfner names the governor and 15 other generals as present at the conference or taken prisoner, 16 in all, the number of generals Bodart has released on parole (our count and comparison); the 20 generals of Ney and the 31st Bulletin are kept as given. The sentence on the Rhine opens the third paragraph of Foucart's footnote; the paragraph between was not transcribed, and the rest of the third paragraph, seen only in the OCR, goes on in Roguet's first person, so it is read as his. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength, and '16 generals and 800 officers were released on parole'; 'besides the 577 guns the French took 1 million pounds of powder, 80,000 filled bombs, 54 flags, 5 standards'; 'according to Marshal Ney's report, 22,000 men of all arms, 20 generals and 800 officers were taken prisoner in Magdeburg, 700 cannon, 1 million pounds of powder, 80,000 filled bombs, iron in abundance, a pontoon train, 54 flags and 5 standards and several silver trumpets were taken, and in the arsenal there were also found 346 foreign flags and 10 such'; 'standards'; 'among the guns taken were 39 position guns of the field artillery'; 'of generals there had been present at the conference besides the governor: Count Wartensleben, Renouard, Tschepe, Alvensleben, Schack and Schimonski as active generals; General Count Kunheim and General Holtzendorf as sick and wounded'; 'in addition the generals Müffling, Kaufberg, Ernest, Wedell, Bünting, Reitzenstein and Count Henckel were taken prisoner, some seriously ill, some wounded'; 'Marshal Ney to the Emperor. Magdeburg, 11 November 1806'; 'the 4 columns were equalised in strength as far as possible; each of them exceeded 4,000 men, so that, including 2,000 artillerymen, 400 cuirassiers, 20 generals and about 800 officers, the whole can be put without exaggeration at 22,000 men. I have in my hands 54 flags of in-'; 'fantry and 5 standards; others were broken; I shall await Your Majesty's orders to send them to you'; 'the fortress contains 700 guns, a million livres of powder, a very great quantity of cast iron, a train of 90 pontoons and flour'; '30th Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Berlin, 10 November 1806'; '16,000 men, nearly 800 guns, magazines of every kind fall into our power'; '31st Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Berlin, 12 November 1806'; 'we have 20 generals, 800 officers, 22,000 prisoners, among whom 2,000 artillerymen, 54 flags, 5 standards, 800 guns, a million of powder, a great bridge train and an immense matériel of artillery'; 'I was designated, says General Roguet in his Memoirs, for the chore of leading the prisoners... The Marshal gave me 18 companies of the various regiments of the army corps, commanded by 3 chefs de bataillon, and 2 pieces of artillery; I kept the latter only 2 days. claims.value: Bodart places Magdeburg, a town in Prussia and capital of the province of Saxony, on the Elbe. Höpfner: by the works undertaken since the end of April 1806 the main fortress and the Stern and Thurm redoubts had been palisaded, many works of the outer enceinte linked by palisades, their salients bonneted and the ditches closed at their outlet to the Elbe, so that with any serious resistance the fortress could be taken only by a formal attack; only the suburbs could not resist long, and the entrenchments near them were to hold the enemy only until the inhabitants had saved their belongings, after which the suburbs were to be burned, though their many massive ruins would still block the view. Buildings that hindered the defence of the Sudenburg and Neustadt were pulled down from the 29th and the rest burned that night. On the right bank the garrison foraged towards the Herrenkrug, Kolbert set fire to the villages of Krakau and Prester, and the French posts were pushed to 12—1500 paces from the glacis, with supports at Biederitz, Alt- and Neu-Königsborn, Menz, Gübs and Pechau and reserves at Gerwisch, Woltersdorf, Nedlitz and Gommern; on the left bank Marchand commanded the position upstream, with his quarters at Gr. Ottersleben, and Vandamme downstream at Olvenstädt. Ney: the extent of the fortifications was immense; the bridges at Schönebeck and over the old Elbe at Plötzky let his corps cross without being disturbed; Friedrichstadt lay on the right bank, where Colbert surrounded the villages of Crakau and Prester and the farms nearer the place; Colbert's posts stood one and a half cannon ranges from the place, and Vandamme's posts were entrenched within musket range of Neustadt; on 7 November Colbert, with his headquarters at Gommern, commanded on the right bank, Marchand was at Gross-Ottersleben and Vandamme had his headquarters at Olvenstadt, his left resting on the Elbe; works of the place protected Sudenburg and the Closterberg; and the musketry and cannonade of almost every night were between Neustadt and Diesdorf.
claims.rationale: Location and works as described, read from the page images. No plan of Magdeburg was inspected (Ney's plan of the blockade, sent on 7 November, was not seen), and where each work stood is taken only from the narratives. Ney gives the distance of the posts in cannon ranges and Höpfner in paces; they are not converted. English renderings (ours): Bodart, '(town in Prussia, on the Elbe, capital of the province of Saxony)'; 'despite the earlier, highly dilapidated state and the faulty construction of the works, Magdeburg had nevertheless been brought, by the corrective works undertaken since the end of April 1806 and by the activity of the engineer of the place, Captain Kleist, to the point that the whole main fortress and the Stern and Thurm redoubts had received a sound palisading, all the barriers had been hung, the barricades and communication bridges finished, all damaged and missing parapets put in order, many works of the outer enceinte linked together by strong palisadings, their salients bonneted and the ditches closed at their outlet to the Elbe, and in general the fortress was in such a state that, with any serious resistance, it could be taken only by a formal attack'; 'only the suburbs were not in a position to offer a long resistance. But the intention was only to hold up the enemy by the entrenchments built near them until the inhabitants had found time to save their belongings. Then the suburbs were to be burned down, although the many massive ruins would still block the free view'; 'on the 29th they began to have some buildings pulled down that hindered the defence of the Sudenburg and the Neustadt; the rest was burned down in the night. The enemy'; 'on the 31st the garrison made a foraging expedition along the right bank of the Elbe towards the Herrenkrug'; 'General Kolbert, who commanded on the right bank, gathered in the following night 600 men of light infantry, 2 companies of voltigeurs and 2 squadrons, attacked the Prussian outposts at 3 o'clock in the morning of 1 November, drove them back into the fortress and set fire to the villages of Krakau and Prester'; 'the French posts on the right bank were now pushed forward to a distance of 12—1500 paces from the glacis, the supports in Biederitz, Alt- and Neu-Königsborn, Menz, Gübs and Pechau, reserves at Gerwisch, Woltersdorf, Nedlitz and Gommern'; 'on the left bank General Marchand commanded the position upstream and had his quarters in Gr. Ottersleben, General Vandamme downstream at Olvenstädt'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 3 November 1806'; 'General Vandamme's division is absolutely insufficient to blockade Magdeburg on both banks of the Elbe, the extent of the fortifications being immense. I have gone over all the positions that it is indispensable to occupy: those of the right bank require fewer men, yet there is not a quarter of the troops needed at that point; and in case of a sortie General Colbert would be forced to fall back on Pechau and Gommern while awaiting the help I would send him from the 2nd division'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 25 October 1806'; 'the bridge at Schönebeck is perfectly established, as is the one over the old Elbe at Plötzky; this construction gives me the means of crossing the river with my army corps without the enemy being able in any way to disturb me'; 'daily report on the blockade of Magdeburg. Schönebeck, 2 November 1806'; 'on the 31st the enemy made a sortie by Friedrichstadt, on the right bank of the Elbe; it was made up of about 600 infantry, 50 cuirassiers and 2 guns. The enemy, after forming up in line between Crakau and Prester, carried off 6 wagons of forage and went back into the place immediately afterwards'; 'in the night of the 31st to 1 November General Colbert, with 600 men of the 6th light and 2 voltigeur companies of the 39th, supported by 1 squadron of hussars and chasseurs and 2 four-pounders, approached Friedrichstadt out of cannon range and surrounded the villages of Crakau and Prester, as well as all the farms nearer the place'; 'General Colbert's posts are at one and a half cannon ranges from the place, and the service is done so that nothing can come out of it. His main posts occupy Biederitz, Alt- and Neu-Königsborn, Menz, Gübs, Zippeleben and Pechau'; 'on the 29th the same cannonade by the enemy on the posts of General Vandamme, entrenched within musket range of Neustadt: neither killed nor wounded'; 'if the works of the place that protect Sudenburg and Closterberg prevent us from keeping these 2 points, they will be set on fire, so that the enemy cannot draw any resource from them and is obliged to take in their population, which is already too considerable in Magdeburg for us not to hope for a general revolt if I receive some mortars to bombard the town'; 'Marshal Ney'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 7 November 1806'; 'General Colbert, whose headquarters are at Gommern, commands on the right bank'; 'General Marchand is established at Gross-Ottersleben'; 'General Vandamme has his headquarters at Olvenstadt, resting his left on the Elbe'; 'musketry and cannonade are repeated almost every night between Neustadt and Diesdorf, which tired the garrison of Magdeburg extremely. I have signal rockets fired twice each'.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian), in Höpfner: the fortress had 577 guns and abundant ammunition but no miners; there was bread flour for 3 months and, in this trading town, no lack of grain, but the governor had neglected to bring in fresh meat and other provisions from the right bank in the 10 days from 18 to 27 October. The bearer of Ney's summons of 23 October reported little siege artillery but 40 to 50 field pieces; the Emperor wrote on 7 November, after ordering Ney to bombard Magdeburg, that all the letters from Stettin asserted that 'the place' was not provisioned and lacked the most important things; the 29th Bulletin put much artillery, considerable magazines and many regimental chests in the fortress, but Ney wrote on 11 November that by his information the regimental chests had followed Prince Hohenlohe's corps on its passage through Magdeburg, and that no trace of the Prince of Hesse's treasure had yet been found. Side A (French): Ney wrote on 25 October that his corps's provisions were assured. He asked for mortars on 30 October, and on 2 November the 4 he had asked of General Clarke arrived with their supply (Höpfner has 4 mortars brought from Erfurt); General Marchand wrote that he had no means to have the ladders shod. The Emperor ordered on 7 November 6 twenty-four-pounders and 2 mortars sent from Wittenberg, noting powder and bombs in quantity at Dresden and 500 milliers of powder at Wittenberg; on 8 November Ney wrote that he had not thought he should countermand that artillery before the capitulation was signed, and would do so then.
claims.rationale: Höpfner, Ney's and Marchand's letters, the Emperor's letter and the 29th Bulletin, read from the page images. Side B's stores were set before the investment; side A's mortars came from Ney's own requests and the Emperor's orders; one claim carries one phase, so it is unresolved. Old measures are kept as printed. The stores found at the capitulation are in claim side-b-losses. Whether the Emperor's guns had arrived by the capitulation is not shown. The sentence on the letters from Stettin does not name the place; it follows the order to bombard Magdeburg and is read as about Magdeburg only on that ground. The Bulletin's regimental chests and Ney's later information differ; both are kept. English renderings (ours): 'the fortress had 577 guns, abundant ammunition, 20,339 men of infantry, 2110 men of actual artillerymen, 510 men of cavalry, 1159 men of the pontoon and other trains, together 24,118 men and 6563 horses, so that a'; 'disproportionately small cavalry and no miners at all were present, a want by which an essential means of defence was withdrawn from the fortress'; 'of bread flour there was a stock for 3 months; of grain there could be no lack, given the great stores in this trading town; on the other hand the governor had neglected, in the 10 days from 18 to 27 October, when the complete investment first took place, to supply himself from the rich country on the right bank of the Elbe with sufficient fresh meat and the other provisions, for which the confusion in the fortress until the complete departure of the Hohenlohe troops may at first have been to blame'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Klein Ottersleben, 23 October 1806'; 'the adjutant-commandant who bore my summons asserts that there are at least 8,000 men in the place, little siege artillery but 40 to 50 field pieces, a regiment of cuirassiers and a strong detachment of hussars'; 'the Emperor to Marshal Ney. Berlin, 7 November 1806'; 'I am ordering General Lemarois, who is at Wittenberg, to send you 6 twenty-four-pounders and 2 mortars with their equipment and supply. We have powder and bombs in quantity at Dresden. You have gunners who can serve this matériel. Bombard Magdeburg'; 'all the letters from Stettin assert that the place is not provisioned and lacks the most important things'; '29th Bulletin of the Grande Armée'; 'Berlin, 9 November 1806'; 'there are in this fortress much artillery, considerable magazines, 16,000 men belonging to more than 70 battalions, and many regimental chests'; 'Marshal Ney to the Emperor. claims.value: Ney wrote on 2 November that he had intelligences in the place with persons who waited only for his bombs to force the governor to capitulate, and that despite the questioning of the deserters who arrived daily he had no very precise figure for the garrison. On 23 October General Wartensleben had told adjutant-commandant Lefol in confidence that he hoped to bring the governor to reason if a few shells were fired on the place (Höpfner gives Wartensleben's words to the French parlementaire from Ney's report). Ney had the Closterberg reconnoitred, and his engineers worked for 4 days on a plan of the blockade, which he sent on 7 November. His parleys over 2 days with civil and military officials of the town convinced him that a simple bombardment would bring the place down (3 November). It was known, he wrote, that the garrison was tired of its service; deserters and prisoners said it had only one night of rest, and the sick were said to number 1,800. Deserters kept coming in: 11 on 3 November, one on the 4th and 5 on the 6th. General Marchand judged on 2 November that Lieutenant General Kleist probably wanted only a plausible reason to surrender honourably, which only a few bombs thrown into the town could give him, and that until then an old soldier like him could not hear of surrendering a place such as Magdeburg. The Emperor wrote on 7 November that all the letters from Stettin asserted that the place, not named in the sentence, was not provisioned (claim means-and-supply). The French estimates of the garrison are in claim side-b-strength-french.
claims.rationale: Side A's letters and report, read from the page images, with Höpfner's. Whether Ney's intelligences in the place were the officials he parleyed with is not shown. English renderings (ours): 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 2 November 1806'; 'I had the honour of writing to you on 30 October and asking you for some mortars to bombard Magdeburg; it would be all the more essential for me to have them at my disposal as the persons with whom I have intelligences in the place are only waiting for the moment when I have had bombs thrown, to force the governor, Count Kleist, to capitulate'; 'the strength of the garrison of Magdeburg is put today at 15,000 men; it has been impossible until now to obtain very precise information on this, despite the questioning to which the deserters, who arrive every day in fairly large numbers, have been subjected'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Klein Ottersleben, 23 October 1806'; 'General Wartensleben, sent by the King of Prussia to this governor, told adjutant-commandant Lefol in confidence that he hoped to succeed in making him listen to reason if a few shells were fired on the place'; 'for the rest the governor was a proud, hard man, feared by his subordinates, who at this time, however, had turned his confidence chiefly to General Count Wartensleben, who had stayed behind in the fortress, who seems early on to have wished for a speedy surrender and, according to Marshal Ney's report to Napoleon, is said to have told the French parlementaire, who complained to him of the old governor's obstinacy, as early as 23 October: "First throw plenty of bombs and shells into the town, and the obstinate governor will surely change his mind."'; 'daily report on the blockade of Magdeburg. Schönebeck, 2 November 1806'; 'I have had the Closterberg reconnoitred; I hope to be able to carry it by a coup de main; at the same time Sudenburg and Neustadt will be escaladed'; 'it is known that the garrison is tired of its service; it will be still more so through the alarms that we give it from time to time'; 'Marshal Ney'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. claims.value: Höpfner: Ney sent the governor, through the former Rittmeister Willisen, burgomaster of Staßfurth, the French Bulletin containing the capitulation of Prenzlau, and had the impossibility of relief put to him; his summons of the 5th again recalled the misfortunes of the Prussian army and the impossibility of relief. The governor answered that he could agree to nothing until he had convinced himself of the army's dissolution by sending a Prussian officer. On 6 November Major Wedell of the Leib-Kürassier regiment, taken at Prenzlau, came in with Ney's envoys and gave the governor's meeting an account of the army's march to the Oder, and Kleist said Wedell had convinced him that relief was hopeless; the engineer of the place told him that the enemy had as yet prepared nothing for a siege. Ney wrote that he had had the orders of the day announcing the capture of Prince Hohenlohe's corps and the surrender of Stettin brought into the town and spread there; that the governor wished to send an officer to Berlin to learn the situation of the Prussian army before deciding on defence or capitulation; and that Baron de Williben, sent by the province's civil authorities to ask that the place not be bombarded, had tried in vain to convince Kleist that the obstinacy of the defence was pointless.
claims.rationale: Side B's history and Ney's letters, read from the page images. Höpfner's footnote says Ney's report speaks of a former Oberstlieutenant and the records of the inquiry into the capitulation of Magdeburg of a Rittmeister Willisen; Ney's letter of 3 November calls Williben a former lieutenant colonel (claim side-b-strength-french). claims.value: Side A (French): on 23 October Ney set out to seize all the communications reaching Magdeburg on the right bank. On 2 November he asked the major general whether the Emperor intended the bombardment to be tried or a simple blockade, and whether he might use every means to reduce the garrison by force or by negotiation; on 3 November, whether to keep to a simple blockade, to bombard, or to negotiate an armistice of 15 days or a month so as to take half his troops to Berlin. His daily report of 2 November planned to carry the Closterberg by a coup de main and at the same time escalade Sudenburg and Neustadt, setting fire to Sudenburg and the Closterberg if the works of the place prevented holding them, so that the enemy could draw no resources from them and would have to take in their population, and hoped for a general revolt in the town if he received mortars; General Marchand urged him that the only aim was the taking of Magdeburg, for which bombs were needed, and that the Closterberg was not worth a hundred grenadiers if it would not hasten that by a quarter of an hour. The Emperor wrote on 7 November: bombard Magdeburg, with red-hot shot to set the town on fire; tell the governor that a siege train had arrived, that the town would be burned and sacked and that there would be no capitulation for the officers; and, if they ever doubted the capture of Küstrin and Stettin, he saw no objection to one of their officers going by Berlin to Küstrin and Stettin and back to Magdeburg to assure them of the position. He imagined that Ney would have Magdeburg before 15 November; his troops had entered Poland, the Russians had not yet entered it on 1 November and would probably be met in the first days of December, and he wished Ney rid of Magdeburg so as to be on the Vistula about that time. He ordered all wagons and baggage searched, saying Ney would find part of the Prince of Hesse-Cassel's treasure and many regimental chests at Magdeburg. By Höpfner, Ney told the governor on the 5th that the bombardment had only been meant to prove that he had the means to reduce Magdeburg to ashes, and he expected to find the Elector of Hesse's treasure there. On 8 November Ney meant to leave the 6th light and the 15th dragoons at Magdeburg and set out for Berlin on the 13th, and promised every precaution so that the Hesse-Cassel treasure, if it was in the place, should not escape.
claims.rationale: Ney's letters and report, Marchand's letter and the Emperor's, read from the page images, with Höpfner's. The aims came both from Ney and from the Emperor's orders, so the phase is left unresolved. The Emperor's letter of 7 November is dated after Ney's trial bombardment of the night of 4 to 5 November, and says he had already let Ney know that the bombardment should keep increasing; that earlier letter was not read, and when the letter of 7 November reached Ney is not shown. English renderings (ours): 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Klein Ottersleben, 23 October 1806'; 'I have the honour to report to Your Highness that I am having a bridge of boats built at Schönebeck; as soon as this operation is finished, I shall cross the Elbe to seize on the right bank of that river all the communications that lead to Magdeburg'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 2 November 1806'; 'my responsibility requires me to ask Your Highness to answer the following questions with precise instructions'; 'is it the Emperor's intention that the bombardment be attempted, or must I confine myself to the simple blockade?'; 'am I authorised to use all the means in my power to reduce the garrison, either by force or by way of negotiations?'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 3 November 1806'; 'if the Emperor wishes me to leave the Vandamme division before Magdeburg and go to Berlin with the rest of my troops, I see no other means of fulfilling his intentions, without compromising that division, than to negotiate with the governor, Count Kleist, an armistice that would put this place in a state of blockade, without any kind of communication with the outside, for a fixed period of 15 days or a month. I could succeed in this negotiation'; 'I beg Your Highness to let me know which course I am to take: either to confine myself to a simple blockade, or to bombard the place, or finally to negotiate an armistice so as to withdraw half my troops and send them to Berlin'; 'daily report on the blockade of Magdeburg. Schönebeck, 2 November 1806'; 'I have had the Closterberg reconnoitred; I hope to be able to carry it by a coup de main; at the same time Sudenburg and Neustadt will be escaladed'; 'if the works of the place that protect Sudenburg and Closterberg prevent us from keeping these 2 points, they will be set on fire, so that the enemy cannot draw any resource from them and is obliged to take in their population, which is already too considerable in Magdeburg for us not to hope for a general revolt if I receive some mortars to bombard the town'; 'Marshal Ney'; 'General Marchand to Marshal Ney. Benekenbeck, 2 November 1806'; 'I think that before making any serious enterprise against the Closterberg one will have to think twice. If the occupation of that post cannot advance the taking of Magdeburg by a quarter of an hour, I think that one should not then risk losing a hundred or so grenadiers to carry it'; 'here the only result one can set oneself is the taking of Magdeburg. For that, bombs are needed. All the rest does nothing to advance the single aim'; 'the Emperor to Marshal Ney. Berlin, 7 November 1806'; 'I am ordering General Lemarois, who is at Wittenberg, to send you 6 twenty-four-pounders and 2 mortars with their equipment and supply. We have powder and bombs in quantity at Dresden. You have gunners who can serve this matériel. Bombard Magdeburg'; 'I have let you know that the bombardment should always go on increasing. Serve the pieces with red-hot shot, so as to set fire to the town'; 'do not be slow to inform me that Magdeburg has surrendered or is on fire'; 'you will not fail to let the governor know that a siege train has reached you from Dresden; that with 100 pieces of artillery and the engineer and artillery officers you have, the place will soon be taken; that in 8 days you will have crossed the ditch and made the breach; that the town will be burned and sacked; that once it comes to that, there will be no capitulation for the officers; that this resistance is pointless, for my armies are on the Vistula, and that Küstrin and Stettin are taken'; 'if they ever doubted'; 'this capture, I would see no objection to one of their officers going by Berlin to Küstrin and to Stettin and coming back to Magdeburg to assure them of the position of things'; 'I imagine that you will have Magdeburg before 15 November'; 'my troops have entered Poland'; 'the Russians had not yet entered it on 1 November'; 'it is probable that we shall meet them in the first days of December'; 'you feel how much I wish you to be rid of Magdeburg, so as to be on the Vistula about that time'; 'you will find at Magdeburg part of the treasure of the Prince of Hesse-Cassel and many regimental chests. Let nothing escape you; to that end have all the wagons and baggage searched, and leave the officers only what truly belongs to them'; 'on the afternoon of the 5th Marshal Ney summoned the fortress again, with the remark that by the bombardment he had only wanted to prove that he possessed the means to reduce Magdeburg to ashes; at the same time he again recalled the misfortunes of the Prussian army and the impossibility of a relief, and asked the governor to have regard for the unfortunate 25,000 inhabitants, who would be exposed to the misfortune of a bombardment to no benefit for the state' (pp. 333-334); 'the marshal expected to find the treasure of the Elector of Hesse in Magdeburg and took every conceivable pains that it should not escape the hands of the French'; 'Marshal Ney to the Emperor. Schönebeck, 8 November 1806'; 'my intention, unless Your Majesty orders otherwise, is to leave at Magdeburg the 6th light infantry and the 15th dragoons, which stayed at Brünswick, and to leave on the 13th with the rest of my army corps for Berlin'; 'Marshal Ney to the Emperor. Schönbeck, 8 November 1806' (his second letter of that date); 'no measures will be neglected for the discovery and preservation of the objects that must belong to Your Majesty; above all I shall exhaust every precaution so that, if the Prince of Hesse-Cassel indeed has part of his treasure in the place, it cannot escape us'.
