claims.value: Side B (Prussian), in Höpfner: the fortress had been readied so that, with any serious resistance, only a formal attack could take it, while the suburbs were to hold the enemy only until the inhabitants had saved their belongings and then be burned; but the governor had too little confidence in his men to bring himself to an active defence, would agree to nothing until an officer had confirmed the army's dissolution, and in the end said he must capitulate out of humanity, while the engineer held that the fortress could hold 4—5 weeks after the opening of the trenches and all the generals except Wartensleben were more or less averse to surrender. Höpfner says the inhabitants' disposition gave no suspicion that they would hinder the defence. Ney wrote that on 23 October Kleist gave his word not to thwart French movements out of range of his cannon; on 7 November, that the day after the trial bombardment the burghers had gathered under the governor's windows and threatened him with revolt if the place were not surrendered; and on 8 November, that there were two parties in the place, the magistrates and inhabitants wishing to capitulate and the officers insisting on resistance. The 29th Bulletin: after several houses were burned the inhabitants showed their discontent and the commandant asked to capitulate.
claims.rationale: Side B's history with Ney's letters and the 29th Bulletin, read from the page images. Höpfner and the French documents differ on the inhabitants; both are kept. The governor's word of 23 October is Ney's report and is not in the Höpfner passages read. English renderings (ours): 'despite the earlier, highly dilapidated state and the faulty construction of the works, Magdeburg had nevertheless been brought, by the corrective works undertaken since the end of April 1806 and by the activity of the engineer of the place, Captain Kleist, to the point that the whole main fortress and the Stern and Thurm redoubts had received a sound palisading, all the barriers had been hung, the barricades and communication bridges finished, all damaged and missing parapets put in order, many works of the outer enceinte linked together by strong palisadings, their salients bonneted and the ditches closed at their outlet to the Elbe, and in general the fortress was in such a state that, with any serious resistance, it could be taken only by a formal attack'; 'only the suburbs were not in a position to offer a long resistance. But the intention was only to hold up the enemy by the entrenchments built near them until the inhabitants had found time to save their belongings. Then the suburbs were to be burned down, although the many massive ruins would still block the free view'; 'Ney's corps hardly had the strength of the garrison, and at the moment only 900 men of cavalry at its disposal, but the governor had too little confidence in his men to bring himself to an active defence'; 'the governor answered: he could not enter into anything until he had really convinced himself of the dissolution of the army by sending a Prussian officer; until that officer's return, however, he would conclude an armistice'; 'it was all in vain. The governor answered that he held himself convinced by Major Wedell of the hopelessness of a relief, and must therefore capitulate out of humanity'; 'the negotiations were continued. The engineer of the place represented to the governor that the fortress could not be taken by a coup de main, that despite its poor profile it could hold out in a regular siege for 4—5'; 'weeks after the opening of the trenches, that the enemy had as yet prepared nothing for a siege, which needed a considerable time, and that he should therefore not hurry anything at all'; 'except General Count Wartensleben, the senior general after the governor, all the generals had shown themselves more or less averse to the surrender of the fortress'; 'the disposition of the inhabitants of Magdeburg gave in no way any suspicion that, even in the greatest straits, they could in any respect hinder the defence'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Klein Ottersleben, 23 October 1806'; 'M. de Kleist has moreover given his word not to seek to thwart the operations of the French armies provided the movements take place out of range of his cannon'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 7 November 1806'; 'the day after the trial bombardment I had made, the burghers gathered under the governor's windows and threatened him with revolt if the surrender of the place were refused'; 'Marshal Ney to the Emperor. Schönbeck, 8 November 1806' (his second letter of that date); 'the governor raised difficulties up to the moment of signing; there were two parties in the place, that of the magistrates and the inhabitants, which wished to capitulate, and that of the officers, which insisted on resistance. This diversity'; 'of opinions hampered the negotiation and prolonged the conferences'; '29th Bulletin of the Grande Armée'; 'Berlin, 9 November 1806'; 'Marshal Ney, charged with the siege of Magdeburg, had this place bombarded. Several houses having been burned, the inhabitants showed their discontent, and the commandant asked to capitulate'.

claims.value: Side A (French) attacked: Bodart has the French under Ney force the garrison to capitulate after a 12-day investment and a short bombardment, and the 29th Bulletin says Ney, charged with the siege, had the place bombarded. Ney bridged the Elbe to seize the communications on the right bank and summoned the place; by his daily report his troops drove the enemy's advanced posts under its cannon from the 26th to the 28th, completing the blockade, and Colbert surrounded the villages of Crakau and Prester near Friedrichstadt in the night of 31 October to 1 November. Höpfner has the investment of the right bank completed on the 27th, only insignificant engagements until the 29th, Kolbert's attack on the Prussian outposts at 3 in the morning of 1 November, and on 4 November a French attack on the Neustadt, repulsed, followed in the night to the 5th by the bombardment and repeated vain attacks on the Neustadt. Ney's letter of 7 November has the enemy attempt a sortie between 8 and 9 that night and be sharply repulsed while 12 bombs and some shells were fired on the place. Side B's sorties, among them the foraging sortie of 31 October, went back into the place or were repulsed, and by Ney's account took no prisoner.
claims.rationale: Coded A_attacked: side A invested, bombarded and summoned the fortress, and side B capitulated; side B's sorties were counterattacks within the siege and do not make it an attacker. The phase is left unresolved: the passages read show Ney's own crossing, summonses, trial bombardment and attacks, and the major general's renewed order to bridge the Elbe, but no order from above to invest or attack Magdeburg; the Emperor's order to bombard is dated 7 November, after the trial bombardment, and says he had already let Ney know that the bombardment should keep increasing; that earlier letter was not read. Who attacked in the night of 4 to 5 November differs (Höpfner: the French, on the Neustadt; Ney: a Prussian sortie); both are kept. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; '29th Bulletin of the Grande Armée'; 'Berlin, 9 November 1806'; 'Marshal Ney, charged with the siege of Magdeburg, had this place bombarded. Several houses having been burned, the inhabitants showed their discontent, and the commandant asked to capitulate'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Klein Ottersleben, 23 October 1806'; 'I have the honour to report to Your Highness that I am having a bridge of boats built at Schönebeck; as soon as this operation is finished, I shall cross the Elbe to seize on the right bank of that river all the communications that lead to Magdeburg'; 'I have had Lieutenant General de Kleist, governor of Magdeburg, summoned; his answer was negative'; 'daily report on the blockade of Magdeburg. Schönebeck, 2 November 1806'; 'the 26th, 27th and 28th were spent compelling the enemy's advanced posts on both banks of the Elbe to withdraw immediately under the cannon of the place; from then on the blockade was complete'; 'on the 31st the enemy made a sortie by Friedrichstadt, on the right bank of the Elbe; it was made up of about 600 infantry, 50 cuirassiers and 2 guns. The enemy, after forming up in line between Crakau and Prester, carried off 6 wagons of forage and went back into the place immediately afterwards'; 'in the night of the 31st to 1 November General Colbert, with 600 men of the 6th light and 2 voltigeur companies of the 39th, supported by 1 squadron of hussars and chasseurs and 2 four-pounders, approached Friedrichstadt out of cannon range and surrounded the villages of Crakau and Prester, as well as all the farms nearer the place'; 'Marshal Ney'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 3 November 1806'; 'I received today at 2 in the morning the letter you did me the honour of writing to me from Berlin on the 1st of this month, in which you renew the order to have a bridge of boats built over the Elbe'; 'Your Highness will have seen from my earlier letters that this bridge has existed opposite Schönebeck since 25 October'; 'only on the 27th did he complete the investment on the right bank of the Elbe, though still at a great distance from the place'; 'on the 29th they began to have some buildings pulled down that hindered the defence of the Sudenburg and the Neustadt; the rest was burned down in the night. The enemy'; 'did not interfere; in general it had so far come only to insignificant engagements'; 'on the 31st the garrison made a foraging expedition along the right bank of the Elbe towards the Herrenkrug'; 'General Kolbert, who commanded on the right bank, gathered in the following night 600 men of light infantry, 2 companies of voltigeurs and 2 squadrons, attacked the Prussian outposts at 3 o'clock in the morning of 1 November, drove them back into the fortress and set fire to the villages of Krakau and Prester'; 'on 4 November the enemy attacked the Neustadt but was repulsed, and in the night to the 5th Marshal Ney had 12 bombs and also some shells thrown at the Altstadt and the Neustadt from the 4 mortars brought up meanwhile from Erfurt, and had the Neustadt attacked repeatedly in vain'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 7 November 1806'; 'great exactness reigns in the service, and the result is that the enemy, after attempting several sorties, has not managed to take a single prisoner from us'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 7 November 1806' (his second letter of that date); 'in the night of the 4th to the 5th the 2nd division took up arms. The 3rd division was also under arms all night; the enemy attempted a sortie between 8 and 9 o'clock; he was sharply repulsed. 12 bombs and some shells were fired on the place; one house was burned in the town and 2 others in the suburb of Neustadt'; 'the Emperor to Marshal Ney. Berlin, 7 November 1806'; 'I am ordering General Lemarois, who is at Wittenberg, to send you 6 twenty-four-pounders and 2 mortars with their equipment and supply. We have powder and bombs in quantity at Dresden. You have gunners who can serve this matériel. Bombard Magdeburg'; 'I have let you know that the bombardment should always go on increasing. Serve the pieces with red-hot shot, so as to set fire to the town'.

claims.value: Side B held a permanent fortress: Höpfner describes the main fortress, the Stern and Thurm redoubts and the works of the outer enceinte, palisaded and with bonneted salients, and entrenchments built near the suburbs; Ney calls the extent of the fortifications immense. Side A's posts were entrenched: Ney's daily report says the enemy's heavy cannonade on his posts caused no losses because they were entrenched, Vandamme's posts being entrenched within musket range of Neustadt, and on 7 November he reported his troops entrenched in their positions, as were the advanced posts, with cuts made on communications he could not guard and artillery placed to protect the outposts' withdrawal in case of a sortie.
claims.rationale: Coded both_fortified: side B defended permanent works, and side A held entrenched posts under the fortress's fire. The fortress is permanent (inherited); side A's entrenchments were made for the blockade on Ney's dispositions (commander-created); one claim carries one phase, so it is unresolved. A coding that counted only the defended fortress would give B_fortified. English renderings (ours): 'despite the earlier, highly dilapidated state and the faulty construction of the works, Magdeburg had nevertheless been brought, by the corrective works undertaken since the end of April 1806 and by the activity of the engineer of the place, Captain Kleist, to the point that the whole main fortress and the Stern and Thurm redoubts had received a sound palisading, all the barriers had been hung, the barricades and communication bridges finished, all damaged and missing parapets put in order, many works of the outer enceinte linked together by strong palisadings, their salients bonneted and the ditches closed at their outlet to the Elbe, and in general the fortress was in such a state that, with any serious resistance, it could be taken only by a formal attack'; 'only the suburbs were not in a position to offer a long resistance. But the intention was only to hold up the enemy by the entrenchments built near them until the inhabitants had found time to save their belongings. Then the suburbs were to be burned down, although the many massive ruins would still block the free view'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 3 November 1806'; 'General Vandamme's division is absolutely insufficient to blockade Magdeburg on both banks of the Elbe, the extent of the fortifications being immense. I have gone over all the positions that it is indispensable to occupy: those of the right bank require fewer men, yet there is not a quarter of the troops needed at that point; and in case of a sortie General Colbert would be forced to fall back on Pechau and Gommern while awaiting the help I would send him from the 2nd division'; 'daily report on the blockade of Magdeburg. Schönebeck, 2 November 1806'; 'the 26th, 27th and 28th were spent compelling the enemy's advanced posts on both banks of the Elbe to withdraw immediately under the cannon of the place; from then on the blockade was complete'; 'the enemy cannonaded our posts heavily; but as they are entrenched, there were neither killed nor wounded'; 'on the 29th the same cannonade by the enemy on the posts of General Vandamme, entrenched within musket range of Neustadt: neither killed nor wounded'; 'Marshal Ney'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 7 November 1806'; 'the troops are entrenched in their positions, as are the advanced posts: cuts have been made on various communications that the number of my troops did not allow me to guard: the artillery is placed on the flank and on the front of the divisions to sweep the plain and protect the withdrawal of the outposts in case of a sortie; in short, every measure has been taken to cut the enemy off from all communication with the outside and to take from him the means of foraging'.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 330 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Magdeburg war trotz des früheren höchst verfallenen Zustandes und der fehlerhaften Konstruktion der Werke dennoch durch den seit Ende April 1806 unternommenen Korrekturbau und durch die Thätigkeit des Ingenieurs vom Platz, Hauptmann Kleist, dahin gebracht worden, daß die ganze Hauptfestung, die Stern- und Thurmschanze eine tüchtige Pallisadirung erhalten hatten, sämmtliche Barrieren eingehangen, die Barrikaden und Kommunikationsbrücken fertig, alle schadhaften und fehlenden Brustwehren in Ordnung gesetzt, viele Werke der äußern Umwallung durch starke Pallisadirungen zusammengehangen, ihre Saillants bonnetirt und die Gräben am Austritt nach der Elbe gesperrt worden waren, und überhaupt die Festung sich in einem Zustande befand, daß sie bei einer irgend ernsten Gegenwehr nur durch einen förmlichen Angriff erobert werden konnte.

open_questions: Deferred: the capitulation's articles 5 to 18 (Foucart t. II, pp. 790-791); the end of the Emperor's letter to Lannes (p. 795); the paragraphs of Roguet's account that were not transcribed (p. 825); seen only in the OCR, the Emperor's letter to Ney of 9 November answering Ney's of the 7th (p. 794), to whose instructions Ney's of the 11th refers (p. 826), the Emperor's letter of 10 November on receiving the capitulation (p. 811), the major general's orders for the garrison and the march to Berlin after the prisoners' departure (p. 820) and the administration's dispositions for the Magdeburg magazines (pp. 863-866); Ney's plan of the blockade, sent on 7 November, not seen; the records of the Prussian inquiry into the capitulation and Ney's correspondence captured at Gutstadt, which Höpfner cites (Bd. 2, pp. 331, 333); the letter in which, by his of 7 November, the Emperor had already told Ney that the bombardment should keep increasing, not found. No figure seen only in the OCR is restated.

Most consequential gap: side A's strength. Bodart's 16,000 is the only total read; Höpfner says only that Ney's corps hardly had the garrison's strength and had 900 cavalry at its disposal, and Ney's letters give his cavalry and the raid's detachment but no infantry count, while calling Vandamme's division insufficient for the blockade. A return of the 6th corps for late October or early November, such as the fold-out situation tables in Foucart's annexes (after p. 939), could close it.

Disputes kept as separate claims or within them: the garrison (Höpfner's return of 24,118; Bodart's 24,000; at least 8,000, 15,000, Williben's more than 16,000, 20,000 with the sick and 22,000 at the defile, in Ney's letters; 16,000 in the 29th and 30th Bulletins and the Emperor's letter of 9 November, the 29th with more than 70 battalions; 20,000 reaching the Rhine, Roguet); the guns (577, Höpfner's return and Bodart; 40 to 50 field pieces, the bearer of the summons; 800 or about 800, Ney on 8 November, the Emperor and the 30th and 31st Bulletins; 700, Ney on 11 November and Höpfner from Ney's report); the generals (16 released on parole, Bodart; 20, Ney, the 31st Bulletin and Höpfner from Ney's report); the date of the capitulation (8 November, Bodart, Höpfner, Ney, its date line and the 30th Bulletin; the 7th, the Emperor on 9 November) and its hour (at 1 o'clock after an arrival in the afternoon, Höpfner; that evening, Ney); the armistice (the afternoon of the 7th, signed for side B with Renouard, Höpfner; 'last night', Ney, its text signed for side B by du Troussel and Le Blanc); the occupation of the Ulrich gate (the 10th, article 2 and Höpfner; the gates on the 9th, the 30th Bulletin); the night of 4 to 5 November (French attacks on the Neustadt, Höpfner; a Prussian sortie repulsed, Ney); Colbert's raid (2 squadrons, Höpfner; 1 squadron and 2 guns, Ney; the outposts driven in, Höpfner, or withdrawn the night before, Ney); the defile (4 columns from 9 to 3 with 25 cavalrymen each, Ney; 4 columns with 20, Höpfner; 8 columns and 18 companies, finished at 6 in the evening, Roguet); the inhabitants (no hindrance to the defence, Höpfner; the burghers' threat of revolt and a party for capitulation, Ney and the 29th Bulletin); and the regimental chests (in the fortress, the Emperor and the 29th Bulletin; gone with Prince Hohenlohe's corps, Ney on 11 November).

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his sources for this entry were not checked; his 577 guns match Höpfner's garrison return and his powder, bombs, flags and standards the figures Höpfner gives from Ney's report, but his garrison breakdown is not Höpfner's return rounded up); Foucart, t. II (the French side's documents, from the page images: Ney's letters of 23 and 25 October and of 2, 3, 7, 8 and 11 November, his daily report of 2 November, General Marchand's letter of 2 November, the Emperor's letters to Ney of 7 and 12 November and to Lannes of 9 November, the armistice and the capitulation's articles 1 to 4, General Roguet's memoirs in a footnote, and the 29th, 30th and 31st Bulletins); Höpfner, Bd. 2, 2nd edition (the Prussian side's history; in this section he cites Marshal Ney's report to Napoleon, from the correspondence captured at Gutstadt in 1807, and the records of the inquiry into the capitulation of Magdeburg, so his figures from Ney's report are not independent of the French documents).
